questions.q: A requirement says 'a Contact can attend multiple Events, and an Event can have multiple Contacts.' Which pattern does this describe?
options: The hierarchy pattern
The event-log pattern
The junction object pattern
The polymorphic lookup pattern
questions.explain: 'Can have multiple' on both sides of the relationship is the recognition trigger for the junction object pattern -- a many-to-many relationship modeled with a custom object holding two relationship fields.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of the hierarchy (self-relationship) pattern, per this lesson?
options: It cannot be used on custom objects
A very deep or wide hierarchy makes rollup reporting and hierarchy-based sharing more expensive to compute, so depth should match actual business need
It always requires a master-detail relationship
It has no practical cost at any depth
questions.explain: The lesson specifically warns that hierarchy depth and breadth both carry real computational and usability costs, so the pattern should be scoped deliberately rather than modeled as infinitely recursive.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's own documentation say about the Task object's WhoId field?
options: It can only ever reference a Contact record
It represents a human such as a lead or a contact, and WhoIds are polymorphic
It is a standard master-detail field
It does not exist on the Task object
questions.explain: Salesforce's object reference states directly that WhoId represents a human such as a lead or a contact, and that WhoIds are polymorphic -- confirming the lesson's polymorphic lookup example.

questions.q: Why can't you build a true polymorphic lookup field the same way on a custom object as Task.WhoId works natively?
options: Because custom objects cannot have any lookup fields
Because Salesforce doesn't offer a true polymorphic custom lookup field; the common workaround is separate lookup fields per target object, enforced to be mutually exclusive
Because polymorphic fields are only available on master-detail relationships
Because WhoId is actually not polymorphic
questions.explain: The lesson explains that true polymorphism is a platform-specific capability on certain standard fields; on custom objects, the common workaround is multiple single-target lookup fields with validation keeping them mutually exclusive.

questions.q: A company wants to record every service event on a piece of equipment, going back indefinitely, rather than just the current status. Which pattern fits this requirement?
options: The junction object pattern
The event-log (append-only history) pattern
The hierarchy pattern
The polymorphic lookup pattern
questions.explain: Needing to know 'what happened, in order, over time' rather than just the current value is the recognition trigger for the event-log pattern described in this lesson.
